Allocation of mortgage interest deduction between joint homeowners

Two US taxpayers, A and B, own a home together as joint tenants.  They both live in the home, and it is their "main home" for tax purposes.  A and B are not married to each other and never have been, and they each file their taxes as "single".

There is a mortgage on the home, in the name of A and B jointly, and they each meet the criteria to take the 
home mortgage interest deduction
.  They each pay half of the monthly mortgage payments.  Must they divide the deduction equally, or may they divide it unequally if this is advantageous to them?

For example, suppose that in a given year, the mortgage payments totaled $40,000, of which $10,000 was principal and $30,000 was interest.  A and B each paid $20,000.

By default, each of them would say they paid $5,000 in principal and $15,000 in interest, and each would take a $15,000 mortgage interest deduction.  But could they instead say that the $20,000 paid by A was entirely interest, and that B paid the entire $10,000 in principal plus the remaining $10,000 in interest?  That would result in A taking a $20,000 deduction, and B taking a $10,000 deduction.  This might be advantageous if A is in a higher tax bracket, or if A itemizes and B does not.

Pub. 936 (linked above) has a section "More than one borrower":

More than one borrower.
 If you and at least one other person (other than your spouse if you file a joint return) were liable for and paid interest on a mortgage that was for your home, and the other person received a Form 1098 showing the interest that was paid during the year, attach a statement to your paper return explaining this. Show how much of the interest each of you paid, and give the name and address of the person who received the form. Deduct your share of the interest on Schedule A (Form 1040), line 8b, and print “See attached” next to the line.

But it does not specify how the shares are to be determined.

Married Filing Separately - Who Can Deduct Mortgage Interest
 is similar, but in that case the taxpayers are married filing separately, and the mortgage is in the name of only one of them.

References to official information would be ideal.

(Bonus question: is there a legal way for A to deduct the entire $30,000 despite only actually paying $20,000 out of pocket?  For instance, suppose that B gifts $20,000 to A (ignoring any gift tax implications), and A then pays the entire mortgage for the year and claims the full deduction.)

How to react to debt collection claim when the delay in payment is the creditor's fault?

I regularly use services from a company, and the company sends me invoices. I have set up a direct debit authorization (Lastschriftmandat) for this company, and the invoices are paid by direct debit. This has been going on for years.

I was recently contacted by a debt collection agency regarding an unpaid one-year-old invoice (June 2025) from this company. Like all the others, the invoice stated "we will debit the money from your account in the following days". However, in this particular case, the company never pulled the money from my account, so the bill is in fact unpaid. My bank account always had enough money and all other invoices from this company (before and after) have been successfully debited.

I did not notice this at the time, and the company never contacted me about a failed direct debit. I did not know about the missing payment until the debt-collection agency contacted me, requesting payment of the invoice amount and additional debt-collection fees. At that point, I immediately paid the invoice amount to the creditor (not the debt collector), and disputed the claim of the debt collector, arguing that the delay in payment was due to the creditor not performing the agreed direct debit, and that I had fulfilled my obligation by providing the direct debit authorization, so I am not liable for debt-collection fees.

Attempts to clarify this with the original creditor are futile. They do not have a phone number. To written requests, they either respond with unrelated AI-generated text or with pre-made text that contains blatant lies ("after sending you several reminders, we passed the debt to a collector", which is completely false and they do not answer when I ask them for proof of those reminders). From recent reviews of the company, it seems that the company is doing this same thing to other people too.

My greatest concern is this event messing up my credit score (Schufa). I have the feeling that if I pay the debt-collection fees, I will be admitting fault and that will negatively affect my score. Disputing the claim may, however, lead to an uncomfortable path (threats of higher costs, or a lawsuit).

What would be the best course of action if the goal is to avoid a negative entry in my credit score?

Can HealthCare.gov force-change my plan variant mid-year due to an income increase?

Plan Name: Changed from 
Baylor Scott & White Marketplace HMO QHP / Bsw Premier HMO-Qhp
 to 
Baylor Scott & White HMO/PPO/EPO/TRS/Covenant / Bsw Plus HMO
.

ID Numbers: Member ID remains identical; the Group number is almost the same, with a few extra digits added.
